questions.prompt: For a map \(F\) with \(m\) outputs and \(n\) inputs, the Jacobian is
options: the \(m \times n\) matrix of partial derivatives \(\partial F_i / \partial x_j\)
the \(n \times m\) matrix with those partials transposed, by definition
the Hessian of each output, stacked in a row
the sum of the output components
questions.explanation: Rows correspond to outputs and columns to inputs, so the shape is \(m \times n\). The transpose is a different arrangement and is not the definition used here. Each output has its own gradient, which becomes one row; the Hessian of an output is a further derivative. Adding the components collapses the map to a scalar.

questions.prompt: Let \(F(x, y) = (x y,\ x + 2y)\). At \((3, 5)\), what is the \((1, 2)\) entry of the Jacobian?
questions.explanation: The first output is \(x y\), and its partial derivative in \(y\) is \(x\), which equals 3. The \((1, 1)\) entry is \(y = 5\). The \((2, 1)\) entry is 1, and the \((2, 2)\) entry is 2. The product \(3 \cdot 5 = 15\) is the first output, not a partial derivative.

questions.prompt: The chain rule for \(F \circ G\) says that the Jacobian of the composition is
options: the sum of the two Jacobians
the Jacobian of \(F\), evaluated at \(G(x)\), times the Jacobian of \(G\) at \(x\)
the Jacobian of \(G\) times the Jacobian of \(F\), with \(F\) evaluated at \(x\)
the entrywise product of the two Jacobians
questions.explanation: The outer derivative is taken at the inner value, and it stands on the left of the product. Adding Jacobians is the rule for a sum of maps. Swapping the order, or evaluating the outer map at \(x\) instead of at \(G(x)\), uses the wrong point and the wrong multiplication. An entrywise product is not matrix multiplication.

questions.prompt: Put these lines of a chain-rule calculation in the only order that makes each line usable.
questions.explanation: The outer Jacobian is evaluated at the image, so the image has to be known before that line can be written. The product uses that evaluated outer Jacobian, so it is last, with the outer factor on the left. The inner Jacobian is taken at the original input and appears only as the right-hand factor; it does not wait for the image, which is why it is not a separate line. Swapping the factors computes a different matrix whenever the sizes differ. Adding the factors is the rule for a sum, not a composition.

steps: Evaluate the inner map at the input, and name that image y.
Evaluate the outer Jacobian at y.
Form the product with that outer Jacobian on the left and the inner Jacobian, at the original input, on the right.

questions.prompt: Let \(g(t) = (t^2, 3t)\) and \(f(x, y) = x + y^2\). What is the derivative of \(f(g(t))\) at \(t = 2\)?
questions.explanation: The image is \((4, 6)\), and \(g'(2) = (4, 3)\). The gradient of \(f\) is \((1, 2y)\), so at the image it is \((1, 12)\). The inner product is \(4 + 36 = 40\). The simplified composition is \(t^2 + 9 t^2 = 10 t^2\), whose derivative \(20 t\) also equals 40 at \(t = 2\). The value of the composition, \(10 \cdot 4 = 40\), matches the derivative here and is not the general rule; at a different \(t\) the two numbers separate.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The Jacobian of \(F(x, y) = (x y,\ x + 2y)\) at \((3, 5)\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). What is its determinant?
questions.explanation: The determinant is \(5 \cdot 2 - 3 \cdot 1 = 7\). The product of the diagonal entries is 10, which does not subtract the other product. The sum of the four entries is 11. The trace is 7 as well for this particular matrix, but the trace is \(5 + 2\), a different operation that happens to match. The determinant formula is the one with the minus sign.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x + y\). The derivative of \(t \mapsto f(a t,\ b t^2)\) is an expression in the names a, b, and t. Write that expression.
questions.explanation:
The inner velocity is \((a, 2 b t)\). The gradient of \(x + y\) is \((1, 1)\). Their inner product is \(a + 2 b t\). The composed function is \(a t + b t^2\), and ordinary differentiation gives the same expression.
• \(a + b t\) misses the 2 from differentiating \(t^2\).
• \(a t + b t^2\) is the composed function, not its derivative.
• \(2 b t\) drops the contribution of the first coordinate.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Using \(J = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), what is the first entry of \(J \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\)?
questions.explanation: The first row dotted with \((2, 1)\) is \(5 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 1 = 13\). The second entry of the product is \(1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1 = 4\). The sum of the first row is 8, which is the product with \((1, 1)\) rather than with \((2, 1)\). The determinant 7 is not an entry of this product.

questions.prompt: If \(f\) is scalar and \(g\) is vector-valued, \(\nabla (f \circ g)(x)\) equals
options: \(J_g(x)\, \nabla f(g(x))\), with no transpose
\(\nabla f(x)\), ignoring \(g\)
\(J_g(x)^{T} \nabla f(g(x))\)
\(J_g(x)^{T} \nabla f(x)\)
questions.explanation: The Jacobian of a scalar is a row, and the gradient is that row written as a column. The chain rule therefore puts the transpose of \(J_g\) against the gradient of \(f\), and the gradient of \(f\) is evaluated at \(g(x)\). Without the transpose the shapes disagree when the dimensions differ. Evaluating \(\nabla f\) at \(x\) uses the wrong point.

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for the Jacobian and the chain rule?
options: The Jacobian of \(F \circ G\) at \(x\) is \(J_F(G(x))\) times \(J_G(x)\).
The gradient of a scalar composition \(f \circ g\) is \(J_g(x)^{T}\) times the gradient of \(f\) at \(g(x)\).
Jacobians add when the maps are composed.
The chain rule evaluates the outer Jacobian at the original input, not at the image.
questions.explanation: Composition multiplies Jacobians, outer at the image on the left. For a scalar outer function the same rule, written with columns, puts a transpose on the inner Jacobian. A sum of maps is what adds Jacobians. The outer factor has to see the point where the outer function is actually being differentiated, which is the image.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x, y) = x + y^2\) and let the path be \((u, 2u)\). What is the derivative of the composition at \(u = 3\)?
questions.explanation: The image is \((3, 6)\). The path velocity is \((1, 2)\), and the gradient of \(f\) there is \((1, 12)\). The inner product is \(1 + 24 = 25\). The composed function is \(u + 4 u^2\), with derivative \(1 + 8u\), which also equals 25 at \(u = 3\). The value of the composition is \(3 + 36 = 39\), not the slope. Twice the second coordinate, 12, is only the second entry of the gradient.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Newton's method for a square nonlinear system linearizes the map by
options: replacing the map with its Hessian
replacing the map with the constant vector F(x)
ignoring the Jacobian and stepping along a coordinate axis
replacing the map with its affine model F(x) + J(x) (z - x)
questions.explanation: One Newton step solves the linear equation given by the value and the Jacobian. The Hessian is the derivative of the Jacobian, used when the unknown is a minimizer of a scalar function rather than a root of a map. Holding the value and dropping the Jacobian leaves a constant, which has no root to compute unless it is already zero. A coordinate step is a different algorithm.
